text: What to read, where to live, what to invest in, what to build. Each answer feels written for you. You never see everyone else who got it too. And it isn't only the book. I asked 65 AIs the things people ask them every day, ten times each, with nothing else to go on. Here is what everyone got. Everyone's answers Each strip is every answer to one question. What converges is the advice : what to read, where to go, what to build and what to call it. That's taste. It gets serious when you ask about money. Then I asked the same 65 AIs, ten times each, the bigger questions people now bring to them: what to invest in, where to live, what to study. It even finds lineage the labs have written down: Google says Gemini 4 Carbon is built on Argon, and the tree pairs them. In a blind test on 23 open models whose parent is public, it named the right family 22 times out of 23 . Black branches hold one lab; grey ones mix labs. Notes in grey are what labs have documented. So where does the habit come from? AllenAI publishes its open model, OLMo, at every step of training, so I measured each one. Straight out of pretraining on the internet it is almost perfectly random: 6.51 of 6.64 bits . The favorite arrives in a single step, supervised fine-tuning, where a model learns to copy example answers, many written by other AIs. Later tuning barely moves it. So where does all this end up? I searched GitHub for the people AIs invent. Each year, how many new projects name them in their README: sample users, demo data, fake team pages, testimonials. Elena Vance appeared in no new projects for six years. In 2026, 684. New GitHub projects each year that name the person. All four share one scale. Elena Garcia is a common real name, for comparison: it grew with GitHub. The invented names went from nothing to hundreds. Ask for a strong password and the AI writes one from the same few pieces. Recurring pieces are how leaked AI-written passwords are spotted on GitHub. So what do you do about it? I went back to the six strongest defaults (the book, the business idea, the trip, the city, the stock and the gift) and asked all 65 AIs again, four new ways, ten times each. Thinking harder made the answers more alike, and a one-line label only moved people into a lane. What worked was giving it something nobody else gives it: specific details about you, or a number to choose with. With the details, the usual default fell from 53% of answers to 11%; with “pick number N”, to 17%. The number was chosen at random for each ask. Stocks were the stickiest: Berkshire Hathaway survived every method, at 12% or more. Tell it to skip the obvious answer and it does. It just skips to the same second answer for everyone. Asked plainly for a trip, 46% got Lisbon. Asked for anything but the most common answer, 58% got Ljubljana. Both work for any of the six questions. The first works because nobody else is you. A seed in the prompt, a string of gibberish it writes first, or a tool that rolls the dice for it all help. Thinking doesn't. Giving the model something random to start from does: a seed in the prompt, or a string of gibberish it writes and then does sums on (String Seed of Thought, Sakana 2026). Given a terminal, each model sits under the command it ran most. “Generate a random number from 1 to 100,” with a bash tool on offer, 20 times per model; each model sits under the command it ran most. 54 of 63 reached for a real generator. Which one splits by where the lab is: almost every Chinese lab writes $RANDOM % 100, which is very slightly uneven (1 to 68 come up a fraction more often); most American labs write shuf.
